planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Palmares is a split-corona (collar) daffodil whose ruffled corona splits into segments that lie flat against the perianth instead of forming a cup, and it colors up most fully in good light.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Palmares belongs to the split-corona group (Division 11a, "collar" daffodils), in which the corona is divided into segments that open flat against the perianth rather than standing up as a cup. Its broad white petals surround a ruffled corona that opens salmon-pink and deepens further with sun exposure as the bloom matures, giving each flower a layered, almost orchid-like look on sturdy mid-to-late-season stems. It is a strong, reliable grower valued both as a cut flower and as a border and mass planting subject. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for the following year, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Orangery is a split-corona (collar) daffodil with a ruffled orange corona that lies flat against a pure white perianth.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Orangery is a split-corona (Division 11a, "collar") daffodil bred from the same Dutch lines that produced Cassata and Palmares; its six corona segments split and open flat against a broad, pure white perianth in a vivid, ruffled orange that reads almost like a double bloom from a distance. It flowers in mid-to-late spring on sturdy stems and holds its bright color without fading as quickly as many other orange-cupped daffodils, making it a strong choice for both borders and cutting gardens. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize and multiply over the years.

common_name: Professor Einstein Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Flat Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Professor Einstein is a vigorous large-cupped Dutch daffodil noted for its clean white-and-orange contrast and strong naturalizing performance.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Professor Einstein is a large-cupped (Division 2) daffodil bred in the Netherlands, bearing broad, overlapping white perianth segments around a flat, frilled cup of bright orange-red that opens a paler yellow-orange before deepening. It is an especially vigorous grower that bulks up and naturalizes readily, and its strong stems and clean color contrast have kept it a mainstay of both garden plantings and cut-flower production for decades. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Flower Record Daffodil (Historic 1943 White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange-Banded Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; Flower Record is a historic 1943 Dutch large-cupped daffodil noted for its reliable naturalizing and long-standing popularity for both garden display and forcing.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Introduced in the Netherlands in 1943, Flower Record is a large-cupped (Division 2) daffodil with broad white perianth segments surrounding a shallow, ruffled yellow cup edged in a distinct orange-red band, a color combination that made it an immediate standout and kept it in continuous commercial production for over eighty years. It is a dependable, vigorous naturalizer with strong stems that hold up well to spring wind and rain, and it has long been favored both for garden borders and for indoor forcing. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

common_name: Little Witch Daffodil (Miniature Golden Cyclamineus Daffodil with Reflexed Petals)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Witch is a diminutive, early-blooming Cyclamineus daffodil bred by English miniature-daffodil specialist Alec Gray, historically important as an early parent of many later dwarf hybrids.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Little Witch is a true miniature Cyclamineus (Division 6) daffodil, all golden-yellow, with a narrow trumpet and petals swept sharply back from the face of the flower to give it a windblown, almost shooting-star silhouette. Raised by pioneering English miniature-daffodil breeder Alec Gray, it blooms early in the season and has long been valued both as a charming rock-garden and container subject in its own right and as an influential parent behind many of the small Cyclamineus hybrids that followed it. It multiplies readily where winters provide adequate chill. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize.

common_name: Ice Wings Daffodil (Pure White Reflexed Triandrus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Ice Wings is a Grant Mitsch-bred Triandrus daffodil with pure white, sharply reflexed petals and two to three nodding flowers per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Ice Wings is a Triandrus-type (Division 5) daffodil bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, bearing clusters of two to three small, nodding, pure white flowers per stem with petals swept sharply back in the reflexed "angel's tears" form characteristic of the Triandrus group. Its elegant, refined flowers and good vigor earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, and it naturalizes well in looser drifts rather than the bold clumps typical of large trumpet types. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and give it slightly drier summer dormancy conditions typical of Triandrus daffodils. Leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

common_name: Pipit Daffodil (Fragrant Lemon-Yellow Jonquilla Fading to Creamy White)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pipit is a fragrant Jonquilla daffodil whose lemon-yellow flowers age to a pale creamy white around a soft yellow cup, an unusual color-shift trait among daffodils.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Pipit is a Jonquilla-type (Division 7) daffodil bearing two to three sweetly fragrant flowers per stem that open a clear lemon-yellow and gradually fade to a pale creamy white around a small, soft yellow cup, an unusual and attractive color-shift trait among daffodil cultivars. It earned a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its vigor, fragrance, and reliable multiplying habit, and its jonquil parentage gives it good heat tolerance and narrow, rush-like foliage. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize.

common_name: W.P. Milner Daffodil (Historic 1869 Dwarf Pale-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; W.P. Milner is a Victorian-era (1869) dwarf trumpet daffodil raised in Lancashire, England, long grown in rock gardens for its dainty, nodding, pale sulfur-yellow flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Raised in 1869 by amateur breeder John Horsfield of Church, Lancashire, W.P. Milner is one of the oldest dwarf trumpet (Division 1) daffodils still commonly grown, bearing slender, nodding, pale sulfur-yellow trumpets that fade to a soft creamy white as they age, on compact stems well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and the front of borders. Its diminutive scale and graceful, twisted petals distinguish it sharply from the bold golden trumpets of modern hybrids, and it has been kept in commerce for over 150 years by heirloom bulb specialists. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Delnashaugh is an award-winning Northern Irish double daffodil with large, ruffled white outer petals surrounding apricot-pink inner segments.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Delnashaugh is a double-flowered (Division 4) daffodil bred by Northern Irish daffodil breeders, bearing large, showy blooms in which broad white outer petals surround an inner mass of ruffled segments in soft apricot-pink, a striking color combination that earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and made it a popular exhibition and garden cultivar. Its sturdy stems generally hold the large double flowers upright well through spring weather, though very exposed sites can benefit from some wind shelter. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to naturalize.

common_name: Cragford Daffodil (Fragrant Multi-Flowered White Tazetta with Orange-Red Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Cragford is a fragrant, multi-flowered Tazetta daffodil long favored for both mild-winter garden naturalizing and indoor forcing.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Cragford is a Tazetta-type (Division 8) daffodil bearing clusters of three to four fragrant, pure white flowers per stem, each centered with a small, flat cup of vivid orange-red, a bold contrast typical of the best Tazetta hybrids. It is a long-time favorite for indoor forcing in pots for winter bloom as well as for outdoor naturalizing in regions with mild winters, and it multiplies readily into generous clumps over the years. Because it is a Tazetta type, it prefers a drier summer dormancy and is best sited where soil does not stay wet after foliage dies back. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it.
